Parenteral - not applicable; transmucosal forms taken as directed
Use only if clearly needed; prolonged use risks neonatal opioid withdrawal
Excreted in milk; single peri-procedural doses usually compatible, caution with repeated use
Caution and reduce dose in renal impairment; titrate to effect
Reduce dose in hepatic impairment; metabolised by the liver
Contraindicated - profound additive CNS and respiratory depression
Respiratory rate, sedation, oxygenation, blood pressure, heart rate
summary: Fentanyl is a potent synthetic mu-opioid agonist roughly 50-100 times more potent than morphine, used for analgesia and as an anaesthetic adjunct, and for severe/breakthrough pain. It has a rapid onset and short duration when given IV. It carries a boxed warning for addiction, abuse, misuse, life-threatening respiratory depression, and fatal interactions with benzodiazepines/CNS depressants. It is a Schedule II controlled substance and is habit forming.
indications: Short-duration analgesia during anaesthesia (premedication, induction, maintenance, immediate postoperative period)
Narcotic analgesic supplement in general or regional anaesthesia
As an anaesthetic agent with oxygen in selected high-risk patients
Management of severe chronic or breakthrough pain (transdermal/transmucosal formulations) in opioid-tolerant patients

dosage.n: Administered only by clinicians trained in opioid anaesthesia

dosage.d: Up to 20-50 mcg/kg in selected procedures
dosage.n: For major cardiac/high-risk surgery; ventilatory support required
Only in opioid-tolerant patients; not for opioid-naive or acute pain

admin: Administer parenteral fentanyl only where resuscitation equipment, oxygen and an opioid antagonist (naloxone) are immediately available
Titrate slowly to effect and monitor respiration continuously
Transdermal/transmucosal products are only for opioid-tolerant patients - never opioid-naive
Do not combine with benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants unless no alternative; reduce doses
moa: Fentanyl is a selective agonist at the mu-opioid receptor in the central nervous system. Receptor activation reduces neuronal excitability and neurotransmitter release, producing analgesia, sedation, and (dose-dependently) respiratory depression. Its high lipophilicity gives rapid CNS penetration, fast onset, and short duration after single IV doses.

absolute: Acute or severe bronchial asthma in an unmonitored setting
Known or suspected gastrointestinal obstruction including paralytic ileus
relative: Concurrent benzodiazepines or other CNS depressants

preg: Use only if clearly needed. Prolonged use during pregnancy can cause neonatal opioid withdrawal syndrome, which may be life-threatening if not recognised and treated. Single peri-procedural doses carry lower risk.
lact: Fentanyl is excreted in breast milk. Single doses for procedures/anaesthesia are generally considered compatible; monitor the infant for sedation and breathing difficulty with repeated maternal use.
renal: Use with caution and consider dose reduction in renal impairment, as accumulation can prolong effects. Titrate carefully to clinical response.
hepatic: Metabolised primarily by hepatic CYP3A4. Reduce dose and titrate cautiously in hepatic impairment due to reduced clearance and risk of accumulation.

major: Benzodiazepines and other CNS depressants (profound sedation, respiratory depression, death)
Strong CYP3A4 inhibitors (ritonavir, ketoconazole, clarithromycin - increased fentanyl levels)
MAO inhibitors (serotonin toxicity; avoid within 14 days)
Other opioids / mixed agonist-antagonists (withdrawal or additive effects)
moderate: Serotonergic drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, triptans - serotonin syndrome)
interactions.food: Grapefruit juice (CYP3A4 inhibition) may increase levels of oral/transmucosal forms
interactions.alcohol: Contraindicated - profound additive CNS and respiratory depression
interactions.diagnostics: May cause detectable opioids on toxicology; can elevate serum amylase/lipase

monitoring: Continuous respiratory rate, depth and oxygen saturation
Signs of misuse, dependence, or withdrawal with repeated use
counsel: This is a very strong opioid - use exactly as prescribed and never share it
Do not drink alcohol or take sedatives/benzodiazepines with it
Seek emergency help for slow or shallow breathing, severe drowsiness, or unresponsiveness
Keep naloxone available if using at home; store securely away from children
Do not drive or operate machinery; risk of dependence with prolonged use
pk: IV almost immediate (minutes); IM ~7-15 minutes; transmucosal within 5-15 minutes
IV peak analgesia within a few minutes; IM ~20-30 minutes
Terminal half-life approximately 3-7 hours (context-sensitive; longer with infusions)
Short after single IV dose (~30-60 minutes); longer with transdermal patches (up to 72 h)
Store at 20-25 C; protect injection from light; secure as a controlled substance
pearls: Schedule II controlled substance - HABIT FORMING with boxed warning for addiction, abuse, misuse, and fatal respiratory depression
Roughly 50-100 times more potent than morphine - small mcg doses are clinically significant
Boxed warning: benzodiazepines/CNS depressants plus fentanyl can cause fatal respiratory depression
Rapid IV bolus can cause chest wall (truncal) rigidity impairing ventilation
Transdermal/transmucosal products are ONLY for opioid-tolerant patients - never opioid-naive or acute pain
missed: Fentanyl injection is given by a clinician, so missed doses do not apply. For transdermal/transmucosal prescriptions, follow the specific product instructions and your clinician's advice - do not apply extra patches or doses to make up for a missed one.
overdose: Overdose causes pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression progressing to apnoea, and coma. It is a medical emergency: secure the airway, support ventilation/oxygenation, and give the opioid antagonist naloxone, repeating as needed because fentanyl can outlast a single naloxone dose. Continuous monitoring is essential.
